865073721640f6cec40225a6599a9e1b.text: The Williams Lake Boys Girls Club is holding their annual haunted house Oct. 16 and 17. It was all hands on deck at the Williams Lake Boys Girls Club on Friday, Oct. 16 as the not-for-profit society serving local children and youth got ready to welcome families to their annual haunted house. Iconic Horror is the theme of this year’s event set to provide good scares in addition to popcorn and burgers cooked up by Cariboo Chevrolet Buick GMC Ltd. “We do it for the community,” said regional director of community engagement and fund development Krista Harvey. “It’s something to bring people together and the haunted house is always great. It’s not for everyone because it can be scary but it’s just one way to bring the community together and do something for the community just like our street party.” Independent living coordinator Brooke Hill served as this year’s event planner. She selected the theme based on movies she liked watching growing up that scared her, and believes there is a frightful movie for every generation. “This is my first year independently doing the haunted house, so I’m really nervous,” Hill said, adding everyone had so much fun last year. Planning for the haunted house gets started in July followed by many meetings and securing volunteers in the weeks leading up to getting the club located downtown across from FreshCo transformed. The by-donation event supports programs offered by the club. “We serve a lot of youth in this community every day,” Hill noted. After Friday’s family-friendly evening the Williams Lake Boys Girls Club is ready to provide full-on scares Saturday, Oct. 17 from 5 p.m. to 9 p.m.

National Defence Minister David McGuinty confirms there have been both fatalities and injuries after an incident at CFB Wainwright in Alberta. McGuinty provided the update in a late-night news conference in Ottawa Saturday. “I’m saddened to share that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident on the base. McGuinty couldn’t provide specific numbers on those dead or injured. He called it an “active and delicate situation.” Wainwright RCMP responded to a request for assistance at CFB Wainwright on Saturday around 4 p.m., with early reports that there was a fire at a training area. McGuinty said his understanding is the fire is “still being monitored very closely.” He said they’re currently “working through the details of what actually occurred,” adding there will be “more to say in the coming hours and days.” McGuinty added the Canadian Armed Forces, the Department of National Defence, partners across the federal government including Public Safety, are working with the Government of Alberta and municipal governments. 0de79e5953c2e27e0988be3bc9482872.text: A report released Friday by B.C.’s police watchdog found no reasonable grounds to believe Prince George RCMP officers committed an offence in connection with a man’s death in August 2025. According to the Independent Investigations Office of B.C. (IIO) report, around 4:54 a.m. on Aug. 24, 2025, a civilian witness called 911 to report the sounds of someone “screaming and smashing stuff” in a neighbouring home. First on scene were three officers wearing body cameras who were let inside by the occupants after locating the residence. According to the report, two officers went to a bedroom door, where a person could be heard gasping inside and blood was visible from under the door. The police officers knocked on the door that was locked from the inside. Officers annouced they were police, but there was no audible response, according to the report. “After additional attempts by police to get the (person) to open the door, he could be heard to say, ‘I’m dying’, and said he could not open it,” the IIO report reads. One officer told the person that if they didn’t open the door, the police would kick it. The officer then kicked the door open and it apparently hit the person, who was lying on the floor inside, read the report. “The officers could now see that there was a lot of blood on the (person’s) body, and (witness officer) immediately radioed for an ambulance to ‘start rolling’,” the report reads. The second officer leaned into the room, illuminating it with a flashlight. The report stated that the person “rapidly picked up” an object that was on the floor beneath his left arm and held it up in both hands in the direction of the officer. “The object can be clearly seen for several seconds on police body-worn camera video,” the report reads. “It appears to be a dark brown wooden dowel or stick slightly longer than the (person’s) forearm. b7b0a06ab29c42c7b933233264bd615f.text: Jenifer Kosman is calling on Canada Post to bring back Forest Grove's post office. Members of the Forest Grove community are looking for a new post office after it closed earlier this year. The post office closed at the end of January this year, following the postmaster’s retirement. At the time, Canada Post described the closure as temporary, pending the hiring of a new postmaster. However, almost nine months later, the post office remains shuttered, and the mailboxes have been removed. Since the closure, Forest Grove residents like Jenifer Kosman have had to drive at least 15 minutes into town to pick up their mail from the 100 Mile House Post Office. As a small business owner who relies on the mail to deliver her hand-sewn products, Kosman said the lack of a local post office is more than just an inconvenience. “It’s frustrating because once our post master had gone and retired on us, that kind of left us with nothing. We have a couple of buildings in the area that are possibilities,” Kosman said. “I have heard the (Forest Grove Store) may be interested in putting it back in with them.” Kosman said she has heard from other Forest Grove residents that Canada Post is reluctant to use these possible locations due to the buildings’ age. She noted she has heard there was a bathroom and water issue in the old building that hosted the former post office. When reached for comment, Phil Legault of Canada Post’s media relations said that the postal service is still looking for a suitable location that meets its requirements, noting that this is a “postmaster-provided post office.” While Kosman believes Canada Post has hired a new postmaster for Forest Grove, however, Legault’s comment on the matter was that Canada Post had begun the hiring process to find a replacement. “What we can provide as an update is that we continue to work diligently to resume consistent postal services in the community,” Legault said. “As we have more information, we will share it with local

31de31f15bc2e21e766029cd1d48c5c2.text: *100 Mile Free Press columnist Ken Alexander interviewed the two candidates running for the Thompson-Nicola Regional District’s Area E, incumbent Jim Smith and Challenger Sally Watson. Voting day is this Saturday, Oct. 17.* Sally Watson wants to become the next Area E Director for the Thompson-Nicola Regional District. She also wants to see changes for the Seventy Mile Access Centre (SMAC). Watson noted that the elementary school building where SMAC is now was closed in 2000 and was inspected in 2008, and it would take $500,000 to fix it. She explained that the only way to fund this would be by creating the Specified Taxation area and by billing all the taxpayers for the upgrade. Watson claimed the current Area E Director, Jim Smith, talked to the SMAC board and told them he and the TNRD were working on a situation where the TNRD would acquire the building and SMAC could use it for $1 per year. Furthermore, the TNRD would do the repairs. There is no doubt that the School District wants to get rid of the property as there is no room in their budget for demolition, she added. Watson is concerned that the SMAC executives were told to keep this quiet and that Director Smith isn’t explaining the difficulty of finding the money for the job, she said. The Canadian Community Building Fund allotment for Area E is about $54,000.00 per year, she added. Watson thinks a better idea might be to work with the 70 Mile Community Hall, apply for grants to build a new building beside the hall to make a new home for SMAC. It’s a marriage made in heaven; SMAC makes money and the Community Hall needs it, she said. Watson added, “I’ll do my meet and greets after the election.” Thompson-Nicola Regional District (TNRD) Area E Director Jim Smith wants to be re-elected for a second term. Smith defeated Sally Watson in 2022. Watson is running against him this year. Here are some of the things Smith has done for his consistency during his first term as the Area E director. 5f0c22aacac31c0769f555f9d8231109.text: Seven trustees have been elected or acclaimed to the School District 27 board of education, according to preliminary results from the Oct. 17 elections. Voters have chosen their school trustees for Cariboo-Chilcotin School District 27 following the Oct. 17 election. Fourteen candidates filed nominations for the board’s seven seats. Three trustees were elected by acclamation and the remaining four seats were decided by voters. William Shepherd of 108 Mile Ranch was acclaimed in Zone 2, while incumbent Michael Franklin and Jenny Philbrick, both of Williams Lake, were acclaimed in zones 6 and 7, respectively. Michael Henshall, representing 100 Mile House, won Zone 3 with 345 votes receiving 60.3 per cent of the vote over current board member Camille Macdonald of 70 Mile House. Mary Forbes of Williams Lake, a longtime trustee and the board’s current vice-chair, was re-elected for Zone 5 with 280 votes receiving 64.1 per cent of the vote. For Zone 1, Ella Brown (Elizabeth) got elected with 230 votes receiving 30.8 per cent of the vote, while incumbant Melissa Coates, who joined the board after winning a local by-election in June 2025 was re-elected for Zone 4 with 83 votes receiving 79.8 per cent of the vote. A total of 1,860 ballots were cast across the district in the school trustee election. These results are preliminary and subject to confirmation by the chief election officer. Official results must be declared by 4 p.m. on Wednesday, Oct. 21.

During the third, Blake Collison and Braden Bolt scored each goal. Netminder Ivan Anderson made 25 saves on 29 shots for the Mustangs. Blake Collison earned top honours of the night for creating prime scoring opportunities while Tristan Aidoo named second star was recognized for his crucial plays on the ice. 80dce98f34af82fbfd3ea4b60b7f2727.text: Incumbent Surinderpal Rathor was at home Saturday, Oct 17 where he anxiously awaited election results. Preliminary results from this year's municipal election in Williams Lake. Official results won't be declared until Wednesday, Oct. 21. Also at home Saturday, Oct. 17 was former mayor and challenger Walter Cobb where he too awaited election results. Incumbent Surinderpal Rathor will remain mayor of Williams Lake for a second term following this year’s municipal election. According to preliminary results that were shared approximately 50 minutes after voting closed 8 p.m. at Marie Sharpe Elementary School, Rathor was identified as the successful candidate against challenger and former mayor Walt Cobb. Rathor was elected mayor in 2022 after serving as a city councillor for more than 20 years. Rathor was at home with family, friends and supporters eagerly awaiting for the results to come in, shortly after which he shared a Facebook post. “Thank you for trusting me to continue serving as your mayor. To my wife, family, campaign team and this incredible community thank you for believing in me,” he wrote. “I’m honoured, grateful and ready to keep working for you. Together we can!” In 2014 and 2018 Rathor was defeated by Cobb for the top position. Preliminary results which won’t be made official until Wednesday, Oct. 21, show Rathor securing 2,116 votes (913 advance and 1,203 general) compared to Cobb’s total of 1,026 (530 advance and 496 general). Councillor incumbents Scott Nelson and Michael Moses were also successfully re-elected. New faces set to take up a councillor seat include Ruth Lloyd and Nathan Wiebe with past city councillors Jason Ryll and Paul French returning. City of Williams Lake chief election officer Ross Coupé said there were a total of 3,182 ballots cast. Preliminary results show incumbent Sheila Boehm unsuccessful in her re-election efforts. Coun. Joan Flaspohler, Jazmyn Lyons and Angie Delainey did not seek re-election.

f070aa4c7343b3777d943d3c09045d35.text: BC Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson speaks at an event in Delta on Oct. 18 announcing the party's new 'Thriving Kids' plan. B.C. Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson promises a fully costed party platform will be available later this afternoon (Sunday, Oct. 18). Doerkson was asked about the platform by a reporter at a media event held in Delta to announce the party’s “Thriving Kids Plan.” Doerkson was joined by Conservative candidates from around the region including Delta South’s Ian Paton – whose farm provided the backdrop for the event – and Delta North’s Monica Mohan. Also present were Surrey candidates Garry Thind (Surrey-Guildford), Mandeep Dhaliwal (Surrey North) and Bryan Tepper (Surrey Panorama), among others from the Lower Mainland. • a $500 activity credit – a refundable B.C. tax credit for sports, music, recreation and art camps; • support for families of children with autism, extending autism funding and reviewing changes by the BC NDP to ensure no family loses their funding. “Too many kids start the school day hungry. Too many families are working harder than ever and still can’t afford hockey, swimming, music, or summer camp. Too many schools have playgrounds that are falling apart, and parents spend years running bake sales to replace them. And too many classrooms have become a contest between the teacher and a cellular phone,” Doerkson said. “Here’s the truth: a child who is hungry, tired, restless, or distracted cannot learn. Every parent knows that. Every teacher sees the results.”

5ddba1385e099e656cfc9007b5758cc3.text: Green Party of Vancouver’s Pete Fry is the new mayor of B.C.’s largest city, Vancouver. Fry beat out incumbent Ken Sim, of ABC Vancouver, by more than 20,000 votes as of 11:20 p.m. on Saturday (Oct. 17). As of 11:20 p.m., Fry had 70,183. Sim had 49,780 votes. There had been 106 out of 149 polling locations counted at that point. Fry took to the stage for his winning speech shortly after 10:30 p.m. on Saturday (Oct. 17). At that time, 75 out of 149 polling locations had been counted. Sim made his concession speech shortly after. He was first elected in 2022, beating out incumbent Kennedy Stewart. Council is a mix of slates, with COPE, Green, OneCity and ABV Vancouver councillors. As of 11 p.m., in the lead is COPE’s Sean Orr (51,777), Green’s Annette Reilly (47,854), COPE’s Chloe Leslie (42,554), COPE’s Devyani Singh (41,031), OneCity’s Lucy Maloney (39,756), Green’s Stephanie Smith (38,498), COPE’s Solomon Yi-Kieran (38,013), Green’s Camil Dumont (37,514), ABC Vancouver’s Mike Klassen (36,927) and ABC Vancouver’s Joyce Gillespie (35,218).

2f218671ca8e24295761bba6b839d00d.text: Current RDOS Director Matt Taylor is throwing his hat into the ring to become Okanagan Falls' inaugural mayor. B.C.’s newest municipality has its first mayor. Matt Taylor has been elected mayor of the District of Okanagan Falls. According to Civic Info BC, Taylor received 780 votes to Tyler Johnsen’s 312 and Glen Innes’ 106. The Penticton Western spoke with Taylor shortly after he received the news himself. “I feel good,” said Taylor. “I think it was a decisive result, and I look forward to being able to benefit the community with having some experience in government.” Joining Taylor at the inaugural council table will be Amy Bydal, Allison Symons, Randy Ludwar and Eugene Dettling. A total of 1,207 ballots were cast in the election according to the preliminary results, out of a total eligible electorate of 2,360, which equates to about a 51 per cent turnout rate. “I would like to say thanks to the residents of Okanagan Falls for taking the time to show out in strong numbers for the vote,” said Taylor. ” I would like to say thanks for all the candidates, both at the mayor level and the councilor level, and the teams that worked with them, and obviously I’d like to thank my own supporters and my family for giving me the time.” Okanagan Falls’ residents voted in a 2025 referendum to incorporate as a municipality, the first to be established since 2016. The inaugural meeting of the District of Okanagan Falls’ new council will finish off the incorporation process on Nov. 6.

927450826335d371aa3abd11f5741f03.text: Coralee Oakes is elected as the new mayor of Quesnel in the 2026 municipal elections. A familiar face is taking the reins in Quesnel as Coralee Oakes prepares to steer the city into its next chapter. Of the 7,806 estimated eligible voters in the Quesnel civic election, only 2,539 rose to the occasion and chose to keep a few familiar faces on council. Oakes won the mayoral race with 2,137 votes, defeating incumbent Ron Paull, who received 324 votes, according to results posted by Civic Info BC. The third mayoral candidate, Brian Waters, received 58 votes. Four incumbent city councillors were re-elected, with Mitch Vik receiving 1,066 votes, Scott Elliot earning 1,009, Tony Goulet securing 940 and Laurey-Anne Roodenburg receiving 890. Incumbents Debra McKelvie and Martin Runge did not receive enough votes to be re-elected, with 750 and 725 votes respectively. Newcomers Jeremy Drew and Ryan Adams also earned seats on council, receiving 1,281 and 809 votes, respectively. Drew received the highest vote total among the councillors listed. In an interview with the *Observer,* Oakes said the result came as a surprise and that she is grateful for the support from the community. “I want to recognize that I’m excited for an incredible team of councillors that have been elected. I think there is some great diversity, and I think we have a lot of work to do,” she said. “I very much look forward to getting to work with all of them soon.” According to Oakes, she connected with Ron Paull and thanked him for his many years of service. “I very much appreciate and I am grateful for all of the work that he has done,” she said. “I also wanted to recognize the important role that he’ll play in the upcoming 100th anniversary and so many exciting events that are going to be in the community.” Oakes also recognized all the other candidates that put their name forward for city council, regional district and school district. “We had absolutely top-notch people. c3852c91ac69d15a3117d3aa2b47f311.text: Jillian Merrick was elected mayor of Wells in the 2026 municipal election. Wells is turning a new page as Jillian Merrick takes the mayor’s chair, leading a council with three new faces. According to preliminary results shared by CivicInfo BC, Merrick won the mayoral race with 85 votes, defeating Rocky Nenka, who received 56 votes. Incumbent councillor Josh-Trotter Wanner was re-elected with 90 votes, while newcomers Miriam Dumitra, Elyssia Sasaki and Eric Andersen secured seats with 79, 76 and 70 votes, respectively.

119af2c4a3ffee2179ab44cfd1904ff0.text: Al Richmond is running for re-election as director of the Cariboo Regional District. Two of the three Cariboo Regional District directors from the South Cariboo retained their seats in the 2026 Municipal Elections. Incumbent director for Electoral Area H, Margo Wagner, and incumbent director for Area G, Al Richmond, both comfortably retained their seats. However, incumbent director for Area L, Eric de Vries, was defeated by challenger Dan Parker. Wagner received 81 per cent of the vote, with 229 of her constituents throwing their support behind her. Her challenger, John Kellett, received only 57 votes. Meanwhile, in the 108 Mile Ranch, Richmond received 641 votes, representing 68.9 per cent of the votes, while his challengers Michele Spence and Roz Griston received 255 votes and 35 votes, respectively. In Area L, the race was largely split between the four candidates, with Parker receiving exactly 33 per cent of the vote, or 286 ballots. Incumbent de Vries received 27.1 per cent of the votes, or 240 votes, followed closely by challenger McLean with 26.8 per cent, or 232 votes, while challenger Bo McKinney received 12.6 per cent, or 109 votes.
